newsitem.title: USA: Shareholders OK Boeing, McDonnell Douglas merger.
newsitem.headline: Shareholders OK Boeing, McDonnell Douglas merger.

text.p: Shareholders on Friday ratified Boeing Co.'s planned $16 billion acquisition of longtime rival McDonnell Douglas Corp., clearing the way for the merger to close next week.

At separate meetings in Seattle and St. Louis, shareholders of both companies overwhelmingly approved the deal, which will create the world's largest aerospace company with projected revenues this year of more than $48 billion.
"Today I believe we have been part of making history," Boeing Chief Executive Phil Condit told shareholders who filled an auditorium at the 81-year-old company's headquarters.
"I believe that by working together we will -- this company will -- define the future of flight," Condit said.

The shareholder approval came two days after Boeing agreed to scrap long-term exclusive sales deals and made other concessions to win European Commission backing for the merger, overcoming the biggest obstacle to the plan.
Final EC approval is expected July 30, and the deal is scheduled to close Aug. 1.
Earlier this month, the U.S. Federal Trade Commission gave its unconditional approval to the deal, which was announced Dec. 15.

"Our merger with Boeing represents the best, even the ideal, solution for the future, for our customers, teammates and shareholders," McDonnell Douglas Chairman John McDonnell told shareholders in St. Louis.
The merger creates what Condit called an "amazing, horizontally integrated company" with major interests in commercial aircraft, fighter jets, missiles and space and with few significant rivals.

Boeing's products will range from the 747 jumbo jet to the F-15 and F/A-18 fighters to Rocketdyne rocket engines acquired in last year's $3.2 billion purchase of Rockwell International Corp.'s space and defence businesses.
In commercial aerospace, where Boeing already dominates the world market with more than a 60 percent share of new sales, only Europe's Airbus Industrie will compete for major orders.

In defence and space, Lockheed Martin Corp. can be expected to battle Boeing for virtually every new major government project, including the new Joint Strike Fighter to be awarded to one of the contractors in 2001.
Lockheed, the No. 1 defence contractor, recently announed plans to buy No. 6 Northrop Grumman Corp. in an $11 billion deal, continuing the industry consolidation encouraged by the Pentagon.
Friday's shareholder approval was a mere formality after Boeing and officials of the European Union went to the brink of a trans-Atlantic trade war before cutting a deal hours before the EC vote.
In Brussels, Belgium, the EC's advisory committee on antitrust gave its backing to the deal Friday, saying the concessions offered by Boeing alleviated its concerns.

At a news conference after the shareholder meeting, Condit said he expected "relatively modest rises" in employment going forward and that the merger itself would not have a major effect on the job picture.
He said he thought most of the company's major hiring to meet the increased demand for airplanes was behind it.
Employment at Boeing rose by about 1,900 jobs over the past month to slightly more than 159,000, compared with 147,600 at the end of last year, company officials said.
The acquisition of the McDonnell Douglas will add about 60,000 jobs.

Condit said there were "possibilities" the company would move some production of commercial aircraft parts to McDonnell Douglas' underused facilities in Long Beach, Calif., although he said he did not expect to move any final assembly work.
He said it was too soon to say what would happen to McDonnell Douglas' own commercial jet programmes such as the new MD-95, which has not had a new order since its launch by ValuJet Inc. in 1995.

McDonnell Douglas Chief Executive Officer Harry Stonecipher, who will become president and chief operating officer of Boeing, said the combined company was committed to the Douglas Aircraft commercial airplane unit.
"We will continue to manufacture commercial aircraft," Stonecipher said.
